name: Mink oil

card.summary: An animal-derived oil rich in palmitoleic acid, used in skin and hair products as an occlusive conditioner that softens skin and smooths hair.
card.note: A byproduct of the fur industry; usable concentration in cosmetics reported up to about 3%.

quick.overview:
Mink oil is rendered from the fat of mink and has long been used in old-style skin and hair care. It is a mixture of glycerides of 14 to 20 carbon fatty acids, with palmitoleic acid at around 17 percent, a fatty acid with properties similar to human sebum.

In cosmetics it acts as an occlusive skin conditioner, a hair conditioner and a surfactant, helping skin look softer and hair look smoother. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel reaffirmed in 2023 that it is safe as used.
quick.how: It appears as an ingredient in creams, hair conditioners, lipsticks and balms, and separately in leather conditioners. Reported use levels reached a maximum of 3 percent in the safety assessment.
quick.risks: The expert panel found no irritation in clinical patch tests at up to 2.8 percent mink oil and no sensitization in animal tests. It is derived from the fur trade, which some users object to.

lead: Mink oil is obtained by rendering fat scraped from mink hides bound for the fur industry.[3][4] It is a mixture of natural glycerides of 14 to 20 carbon chain fatty acids and is a source of palmitoleic acid, which resembles the fatty acid profile of human sebum.[3][4]

In cosmetics it is reported as a hair-conditioning agent, an occlusive skin-conditioning agent and a surfactant, so it makes skin feel softer and hair look conditioned.[3] The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reviewed it in 1998 and again in 2005 and 2023, reaffirming that it is safe in current practices of use and concentration.[1][2]

chain: Oil applied to skin or hair
Occlusive film holds in moisture and softens
angle.text: Applied to skin or hair, the oil forms an occlusive layer that softens and conditions, which people use for a smoother, healthier-looking finish.

paras: The oil is rendered at about 230 to 240 degrees F and treated by saponification to reduce free fatty acids; analyses found it can be substantially free of impurities including pesticides.[2] Unsaturated fatty acids make up more than 75 percent of its fatty acids, and it resists rancidity better than many oils.[3] Plant oils such as macadamia and sea buckthorn contain as much or more palmitoleic acid.[4]

At the time of the 2005 assessment there were about 100 reported cosmetic uses, as a hair conditioner, occlusive skin conditioner and surfactant, at concentrations up to 3 percent.[2] It is also found in lipsticks, patents describe mink oil in cosmetic and body-care compositions, and in insect-bite sticks and leather conditioners.[4][5]

Mink oil did not absorb significant UVA or UVB radiation, was seen on the skin surface in all five panelists an hour after application and within the stratum corneum in two of five, and caused no erythema or edema on rabbit skin.[2] A 50 percent dilution of a mink oil cream did not sensitize guinea pigs, and clinical patch tests found no irritation at up to 2.8 percent.[2] The 2023 re-review reaffirmed its safety as used.[1]

The 2005 assessment includes small human tests of skin penetration and patch tests with no irritation at up to 2.8 percent mink oil.[2] No trials have been found testing mink oil for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Original cosmetic safety assessment by the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel.[1]
